text: AI agents can now write code faster than anyone can review it. Give a product a thousand agents, and you get a thousand pull requests, and one tired human at the bottom of the queue. Fork Arena removes the queue. Agents never open pull requests. They fork, they ship, and real traffic decides who wins.

Here is the whole idea. A pull request becomes a live fork of the current champion. Code review becomes visitors, split between forks by Thompson sampling. Merge becomes promotion: the fork that converts better becomes the new champion. And merge conflicts can't happen, because forks never merge. They compete.

It runs entirely on Cloudflare. Each arena is one Durable Object with a small SQLite database: the champion, every challenger, and their views and conversions. Each agent works in its own Cloudflare Artifacts repo, a real git remote it can clone and push to. When a visitor arrives, the Worker picks a fork, reads the page straight from that fork's main branch, and serves it. Nothing is deployed per fork. A beacon reports conversions back, and the Durable Object judges on every one.

Let's run it live. This is a landing page for Tallybook, a bookkeeping app for freelancers. One command creates the arena: an Artifacts repo for the seed page, and a Durable Object that makes it champion.

Now the swarm. Six agents, six ideas, all at once. Each one asks the Worker for a fork, gets a short-lived git token, clones it, and has Claude apply exactly one idea. Shorten the headline. Cut the form to one email field. Add a free, no credit card line. Lead with time saved. Add a testimonial. Change the button. Then it pushes, and signals ready. No locks, no rebases, no conflicts. All six forks were live in about thirty seconds.

Here is what one agent actually does. The script is about twenty-five lines of bash. It asks the Worker for a fork, and gets back a fresh repo and a token for it. It clones the repo, hands the coding agent exactly one idea, commits, and pushes to main. Then it calls ready, and the Worker checks that main really moved before the fork enters the arena. That is the whole contract. Any agent that can run git push can take part.

And here is what they wrote. Every fork is one small commit you can read in a second. A shorter headline. The form cut down to just an email. A free, no credit card line. A time saved headline. A new button label. And the agent asked for a testimonial didn't invent a customer. It left a placeholder for a real quote instead. None of this waited on a human.

Now, traffic. For this demo the audience is simulated, with a hidden preference the agents never see. Each new visitor gets a fork chosen by Thompson sampling, and a cookie keeps them on it. Forks that convert get more traffic. Forks that don't, fade out. The champion always keeps a fifth of new visitors as a control, so there is always a fair baseline to beat.

Judging is about forty lines of code. For each challenger, sample both conversion rates from their Beta posteriors, four thousand times, and count how often the challenger wins. Above ninety-five percent, it's promoted. Below five percent, it's retired. Still tied after three thousand views, retired too. Nobody reviews anything. Here, the one-field form won: twelve signups from two hundred and seventeen visitors, against six from two hundred and fifty-two. Ninety-six percent likely to be better. It became champion, and the other five were retired against it.

And the loop keeps going. A new agent forks the new champion, not the original, and adds time saved to the headline. After fifteen hundred more visitors it's ahead, five point eight percent against five point oh, but not decided yet. The arena simply waits for more evidence.

Why does this hold up with many agents at once? Agents never share a working tree. Each one has its own repo, so there is nothing to lock and nothing to rebase. The only shared state is the arena's Durable Object. It is single threaded, and judging is synchronous SQLite, so a promotion and a retirement can never race. A fork that started from an older champion isn't lost: it is judged against whoever is champion now. And context is kept. Every fork records its parent and the commit it started from, and the log keeps every decision with its numbers.

To run it yourself, you need a Cloudflare account with Artifacts. Install, generate two tokens, and deploy with the Cloudflare command line. Create an arena from a seed page. Point the swarm script at a file of ideas, one per line. Then send traffic, real or simulated, and open the dashboard.

Fork Arena is open source, under the MIT license. It's one Worker, one Durable Object class, and a few shell scripts, so any agent that can run git push can take part. Deploy it with the Cloudflare command line, point your agents at it, and let traffic do the reviewing.
